We conducted a study on a single disk being gradually pushed into a container holding a collection of jammed, uniformly sized disks, all with the same friction and elasticity. Contrary to what happens with numerous uniformly sized disks, we found that when the confined disk is significantly lighter, jamming occurs at lower levels of packing density, particularly in configurations where the disk can move freely compared to when it's always pushed against the others, mimicking a flat surface of the pack. Moreover, we found that this unconventional jamming point is more sensitive to the size of the confined disk, particularly to its curvature and to whether or not it can collide with particles in the pack, highlighting the complexities of jamming behavior.

Recent research has identified multiple types of El Niño and La Niña events, 
characterized by varied precipitation patterns. These phenomena, first observed 
by researchers such as Huang et al. (2013), are associated with a distinct set of 
variables, including sea surface temperature, sea level pressure, and wind speed. 
We have further investigated the sea surface temperature and sea level pressure 
patterns, revealing significant differences between the different types of 
El Niño and La Niña events. These variations, which span multiple years, 
indicate that future climate change projections may be influenced by the type of 
El Niño or La Niña event that occurs.

The elastic regime of materials is often described using non-affine characteristics, characterized by localized deformations within the material structure. This study aims to provide a detailed explanation of non-affinity in the elastic range and present a method for experimentally verifying it in thin films of Lennard-Jones particles. Our analysis builds on previous work involving x-ray topography, but extends to techniques such as scanning probe microscopy and molecular dynamics simulations to demonstrate non-affine behavior. These methods offer a novel approach to quantifying non-affinity and will serve as a benchmark for future experimental techniques capable of detecting non-affine behavior in materials.

Existing research has established the presence of asymptotic states in single-population models. Our work, however, introduces randomness into these models using the Riesz norm in the underlying space of measures. We have successfully demonstrated the existence of a stochastic asymptotic state. Ultimately, by applying the stochastic model, the introduction of a new class of stochastic models can be achieved through a straightforward process.

M. H. Ghasemi and B. Masud's research is referenced in a 2019 paper, which has yet to be fully integrated into the existing fuzzy logic literature. The authors' investigation into the computational complexity of fuzzy logic MTL has a stated goal of establishing whether the problem is NP-hard. This goal is supported by an alternative approach that involves a direct assessment of the complexity of a suitably constructed formula, which is a key component of the solution.

The growth of online content necessitates efficient taxonomy expansion to ensure seamless navigation and search.  Traditional taxonomy maintenance involves laboriously categorizing new items.  We present a method to automatically classify under-categorized web pages based on their text, significantly reducing manual effort.  Focusing on a specific taxonomy - Wikipedia: Sports, our goal is to identify relevant pages for each sport category.  We propose HyperExpan, an innovative approach that utilizes the hyperlinks within wiki pages to provide context and improve classification accuracy.  HyperExExan achieves an 86.1% improvement in accuracy and a 87% reduction in processing time compared to a baseline algorithm.

A comprehensive analysis of electric property predictions in the ATODAD database has been conducted, which includes a wide range of molecules and supramolecular complexes. The set of property data encompasses dipole moments, quadrupole moments, and various electrostatic interaction energies. The analysis involved testing the performance of a variety of density functional and wavefunction-based methods across the entire database, as well as a wide range of basis sets. The results showed that a specific combination of a certain density functional and basis set yielded the most accurate predictions for quadrupole moments, whereas other properties exhibited slightly different trends. The analysis also revealed notable discrepancies between various density functional methods and highlighted the benefits of incorporating dispersion-corrected density functional methods. The outcomes of this study have significant implications for the design and development of certain types of experiments and applications.

In practical industrial environments, tasks are frequently carried out with a level of unpredictability that goes beyond traditional modeling methods. This type of uncertainty is seen as non-deterministic, but it can be addressed by integrating deep probabilistic learning techniques into the control framework. By modeling uncertainty probabilistically, the system can develop strategies to minimize its impact. This approach allows for end-to-end training of tasks with probabilistic uncertainty. This paper examines the feasibility of learning skills in complex robotic environments using an End-to-End Probabilistic Learning (EEPL) framework. This framework enables training of skills in tasks with probabilistic uncertainty using techniques like Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and Monte-Carlo Dropout (MCDO). Experimental results show that EEPL outperforms state-of-the-art learning methods, particularly in tasks involving complex robotic manipulation.

We propose a novel approach to integrate resilience into the PVS (Prusa Verification System) based specification language TCT, enabling automatic verification of resilience properties in embedded real-time systems. This is achieved by defining a 'Resilience Satisfaction Value' that measures recoverability and durability in system responses to fault and overload events. Our 'resilient satisfaction' operator uses a customizable resilience function to assess whether a system response meets its requirements within a specified time frame, even when subjected to unexpected events. This operator can be applied to any first-order formula, allowing us to verify complex resilience properties automatically. Our approach demonstrates that a system can tolerate and mask fault and overload events, ensuring that its responses continue to meet its requirements after such incidents.

Accelerometer networks have the potential to aid in detecting dark matter, 
which is anticipated to interact weakly with ordinary matter, leaving detectable 
imprints in the accelerometer's output data. By analyzing this data, it is possible 
to identify dark matter signals amidst noise. Accelerometer networks can be effectively 
utilized to search for dark matter, which can be modeled as a plane wave, thereby 
reducing the complexity of the search. We have developed a neural network that can be 
trained to identify two-dimensional gratings in data, which can be adapted to detect 
dark matter plane waves, even when the direction of the wave is unknown. This is 
achieved by either training the network to be direction-agnostic or having it take 
direction as an additional input. We have also created a more general network that can 
identify gratings in any orientation, making it suitable for any scalar field, such as 
axion-like particles, which may not have a well-defined direction. By testing these 
networks on simulated data, we have found that they can successfully identify and 
detect dark matter signals, even in the presence of noise.

This paper derives a quantitative asymptotic estimate for $u(t,x)$ in the context of a nonlinear diffusion equation, which is mathematically represented by the equation $u_{t}=\Delta_{\mathbb{H}^{1}}(u^{m})$, within the unit ball of the Heisenberg group for $t\geq0$, with $u$ satisfying the boundary condition of zero and $u(0,x)$ being a nonnegative, bounded function. We establish a profile estimate for $u(t,x)$ under the condition that $m\geq\frac{N+m}{N}$ in the paper 'Profiles for Nonlinear Diffusion Equation in Heisenberg Group', with $N=3$ denoting the dimension of the Heisenberg group.

We analyzed a sample of 111 radio sources, identified by the VLASS survey, and located in the nearby universe (up to a redshift of 0.3), by cross-referencing with the SDSS catalog. This allowed us to study the emission properties of the sources in detail, particularly focusing on the VLASS's L-band data. We developed a method to analyze the VLASS data, accounting for beam size and resolution issues, and used it to derive the low-frequency behavior of the sources' radio spectra, spanning from 2 to 13 GHz. Our analysis revealed that the sources exhibit a specific pattern in the emission index, with stronger emission at lower frequencies. Furthermore, we found that sources emitting more polarized radiation tend to have stronger emission at lower frequencies. Our results align with existing findings from other studies, but also reveal previously unknown connections between radio emission properties and the emission index.

We examine a broad category of probabilistic entropy functions, which serve as security metrics through uncertainty measurements. The first component of this entropy class, $H_1$, is a functional applied to the probability distribution of a random variable. The second component, $H_2$, is a binary entropy function taking the probability as its sole argument. We investigate the most effective ways to combine these two components using parameters that can depend on the probability distribution itself. Our investigation focuses on the constraints that ensure $H_0 = (1-p)\log_2(1/p)+h(\phi(p))$ acts as a valid alternative to the standard $V$-measure, where $0\leq\phi(p)\leq p$ for all $p$. Our primary finding is that any $H\in\mathcal{H}$ can be expressed as $H_0$ with an appropriately chosen $\phi$. This implies a crucial limitation: no security state metric based on the residual entropy class can surpass the $V$-measure.

We have developed a novel approach to derive the turbulent transport operator in the advection-diffusion equation, in terms of the velocity field's auto-correlation function. This operator is represented as a series of derivatives, with its leading terms forming the Kramers-Fokker-Planck operator. Our approach is grounded in a systematic expansion of the velocity field's spatial scales, in contrast to the traditional perturbation expansion based on the velocity field's amplitude. Each term in our derived operator is accompanied by a clear physical interpretation, and we have successfully applied this operator to a two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow, yielding an operator that closely resembles the conventional turbulent transport operator in its integral form.

Fitting experimental elastic scattering data using traditional methods relies heavily on optical potential parameters, which have been obtained from the same dataset. However, these potentials often have limited physical significance and can only be utilized for analyzing the very data they were derived from. A new approach has been developed to address these limitations by parameterizing the elastic scattering amplitude directly, using a theoretical framework that accounts for processes up to the two-photon exchange. This method yields results that can be applied to elastic scattering and also to processes involving single charge exchange, demonstrating applicability through calculations with experimental data from various alpha-actinide systems.

A theoretical model is proposed to analyze blackbody radiation within a two-dimensional conductor of finite thickness, subject to specific boundary conditions. It's demonstrated that under these conditions, certain thermodynamic properties, including pressure and entropy, lose their physical significance when calculated as derivatives of the internal energy. Furthermore, it's proven that adding uniform end-cap conductors to the slab does not alter the total radiation energy emitted by the system. In contrast, non-uniform boundary scenarios are investigated, and it's found that the slab can act as a concentrator of radiation energy at designated locations.

A new approach is presented to protect user privacy in location services that release data in the form of trajectories. Traditional differential privacy methods are ineffective for dependent data such as trajectories, so a two-step approach is proposed. First, it calculates the maximum amount of information any single data point can reveal through a conditionally independent model, such as Markov chains. Then, it reduces this privacy loss while maintaining the model. Next, it extends this step to release multiple data points, such as a trajectory, subject to a privacy constraint, utilizing an efficient algorithm. Finally, it demonstrates the approach on a GPS dataset, proving that it can provide precise data releases, such as predicting user locations, with minimal information disclosure.

Deep learning methods for 2D and 3D point clouds have been highly effective in the field of computer vision, including automotive applications. One critical task is using deep networks to identify current locations based on previous maps, allowing for the accurate estimation of current positions. However, training these networks requires a substantial amount of time and computational resources. A recent approach, known as the 3D point cloud based method, relies on a large database to achieve high accuracy, but it still demands significant training time. A more efficient representation is needed to reduce training time and improve real-time performance. A novel unsupervised deep feature learning method has been developed to address this challenge by extracting key points from a database and using them to create a more accurate representation. This approach allows for real-time performance and has been shown to achieve high accuracy in the field of computer vision.

Functional connectivity research is based on statistical relationships between brain regions, but variability in connectivity estimates can be a result of differences in the brain scanning process and data analysis techniques. A comprehensive review of data cleaning methods used in functional connectivity studies is conducted to assess their impact on the reliability of detecting differences between individuals and groups. Inter-site effects were found to be a significant challenge, but careful data analysis can still provide a reliable measure of individual differences. However, group comparisons are more challenging due to inter-site effects, and standardizing data using methods like ComBat can compromise the validity of these comparisons. Therefore, researchers are advised to use advanced data collection methods that minimize variability and employ sophisticated statistical techniques to model complex correlations across sites.

In the context of the distributed communication model, we have developed efficient algorithms for the challenges of naming and counting problems, specifically focusing on the constraints of non-unique station identifiers and absent broadcasting capabilities. Our innovative solutions can be applied universally across various distributed communication models, including the beeping and oblivious models. Our algorithms are designed to operate within a minimal energy framework, requiring only a constant amount of energy to transmit a single packet. Surprisingly, our beeping algorithms achieve a energy complexity of O(log*n) beeping duration and a name assignment complexity of O(log*n) = Ñ. For the energy counting problem, our beeping algorithms reach an energy complexity of O(log*n) = Ñ. Notably, our beeping naming and beeping energy algorithms are optimal up to a constant factor. In the case of the oblivious model, our energy counting algorithm boasts an energy complexity of O(log*n) = Ñ. In contrast, existing naming and counting solutions are characterized by a higher energy requirement of O(log^2*n) = Ñ.

The effectiveness of positional encoding in positional encoding schemes is well established, but their use in code-mixed text has been limited due to concerns over information leakage from main language texts. We propose novel schemes to introduce controlled information into large language models without compromising the information in code-mixed text. Our approach involves using dynamic positional encoding to dynamically adjust embeddings over time, and a multi-task learning strategy to control attention between tasks. We demonstrate the efficacy of dynamic positional encoding in processing code-mixed text, showcasing its potential to improve task performance.

Using a quasi-harmonic approximation, we've investigated the isotope effect in H$_{3}$S under high pressure. Our results indicate the total isotope effect coefficient, $\lambda$,$\nu$, can be broken down into electronic and vibrational contributions, which are highly pressure-dependent due to volume changes affecting electronic properties and atomic positions, respectively. At 160 GPa, we found experimentally reported data for the superconducting transition temperature of H$_{3}$S and its deuterated counterpart to be inconsistent with calculated isotope effect coefficients, suggesting that the reported values may have been influenced by significant sample inhomogeneity.

This study introduces a novel algorithm for integrating multi-point sensory data into a real-time, D* Lite based motion planner. We've designed a novel algorithm to efficiently process multiple points of interest, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the map and improving the robot's motion planning capabilities. We've established a method to determine the relative positions of these points, and incorporated them into the global map. We've also integrated the algorithm with D* Lite, a widely used motion planner, and introduced a novel method to update the planning horizon. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach through experimental validation, which showed significant improvements in both motion efficiency and real-time performance.

Camera pose estimation is a crucial component of visual odometry, which can be particularly challenging in complex situations. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of data-driven methods that can effectively estimate camera poses. Building on this knowledge, this paper presents a novel approach using a deep learning-based method to predict point correspondences between two views, which are then matched to derive camera poses. A proposed deep learning framework, known as Deep Matching (DMM), combines predictions from multiple deep learning-based correspondences estimators, which are trained to perform on arbitrary images. As a result, the DMM approach achieves superior performance, specifically when estimating camera poses for the challenging task of recognizing the position of a vehicle camera in the night-time. Evaluation of the proposed method on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates its superior performance, with improvements of up to 20% on the KITTI dataset.

This research addresses the challenge of optimizing precoding in multiuser MIMO systems through interference-limited channels, leveraging machine learning to minimize interference and maximize the sum-rate. By combining group LASSO and reinforcement learning, we develop an iterative approach that adapts to interference limitations and constrains precoding. The adaptation of group LASSO reduces interference and enhances performance, while reinforcement learning with a multi-layer perceptron network enables optimal channel selection. The results of our multi-user simulations demonstrate that this method outperforms existing solutions in terms of sum-rate and is effective for interference management.

Given a finite harmonic morphism $f\colon \Gamma\to \bar\Gamma$ between two tropical curves, a semirational function $r\colon \bar\Gamma\to \mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$ can be extended to $f^\ast r\colon \Gamma\to \mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\}$. The definition of the pullback relies on the condition that for any semirational function $r$, the pullback under $f$ satisfies the equation $(f^\ast r)(x) = r(f(x))$ for all $x\in \Gamma$. The computation of the pullback is performed by breaking down $r$ into linear functions on each edge of $\bar\Gamma$ and applying the finite harmonic map $f$ to the parameters of these linear functions. The resulting parameters define the linear functions on the edges of $\Gamma$. The article also explores the relationship between the pullback operation and the properties of finite harmonic maps, as well as the connection between the pullback operation and the concept of divisors on tropical curves.

We analyze Markov processes with no absorbing states under certain conditions (T1-T4) that result in each state type having its distinct quasi-stationary distribution and achieving exponential convergence. This specific analysis focuses on a subset of those conditions that yields a singular quasi-stationary distribution and corresponds to the framework of Doob's h-transform. In the context of the fractional Schrodinger operator with a potential, we demonstrate that the identified conditions are fulfilled. This, in turn, allows us to establish a connection between the ground state of the operator and the quasi-stationary distribution.

Using Chen's integrals of certain cochains, we develop an analog of knot invariants within Stasheff algebras $A_\infty$, which can also be considered as a property of the little disks category. The inclusion of certain cochains enables a level of invariance against transformations in the form of diffeomorphisms for such integrals. The level of invariance is dependent on the specific type of cochains used for insertion into the Chen integrals. The construction of our level of invariance is influenced by the level of invariance used in the context of the Kontsevich theory.

In this research, the scientists conducted elastoresistance experiments on thin films of LiFeAs and NaFeAs, and the superconducting films were created using the pulse laser molecular beam epitaxy technique. They then investigated nematic fluctuations in the superconducting state and the normal state by applying uniaxial strain, and the results showed that nematic stiffness in LiFeAs is significantly higher than that of NaFeAs. Moreover, the researchers observed that nematic fluctuations in LiFeAs are more intense in the superconducting state, and the measurements in the normal state revealed a distinct difference in nematic stiffness between the two materials. A temperature-dependent analysis of nematic susceptibility in the normal state indicated that LiFeAs has a higher critical value of Hubble constant, and the researchers also discovered that nematic fluctuations in NaFeAs are more intense in the superconducting state, and the measurements revealed a distinct difference in nematic stiffness in the normal and superconducting states. A temperature-dependent analysis of nematic stiffness in the normal state indicated that nematic stiffness in LiFeAs is more intense than that in NaFeAs, and the scientists proposed that nematic competition with superconductivity in NaFeAs is more intense than that in LiFeAs.

In this study, we examine two Higgs doublet models of type II, focusing on scenarios where non-degenerate light sparticles and a compressed heavy Higgs sector coexist. We utilize multi-dimensional exclusion limits from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations to explore this scenario, while adhering to theoretical and benchmark constraints. Our analysis reveals that model-free parameter spaces are heavily restricted, but four out of ten widely accepted NDM benchmarks can evade current experimental bounds. This research aims to stimulate further investigations into these theoretically viable scenarios.

To train an agent in manipulating objects, we've developed a novel teaching method that categorizes tasks into two types: purpose-driven manipulation and random, unplanned manipulation. Our approach leverages a single algorithm, which can be adjusted through a 'temperature' parameter to control the amount of directed instruction versus exploratory learning. By using the same algorithm, we can also determine the level of consistency in the agent's acquired skills. Our results, based on a simple yet comprehensive task, show that our method is effective in capturing a wide range of manipulation skills, including both consistent and versatile approaches, and that these skills can be trained in a highly consistent manner.

This research focuses on understanding flavor-symmetric confining vacua of confining, massless, chiral gauge theories based on Sp(N) gauge groups with three types of matter fields in the fundamental representation, specifically denoted as Q, Psi_1 and Psi_2. The primary objective of the study is to establish that the confining vacua of these theories have trivial vacua, which can be demonstrated by analyzing the structure of the theory's matter content and gauge group, and showing that the theory's flavor symmetry group's anomalies match with the theory's vacuum configuration. The research builds on previous studies of theories with mesonic and bilinear fields and extends them to include theories with fermionic bilinears, ultimately providing a comprehensive classification of the theory's possible vacuum configurations.

In this research, we investigate the properties of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations within the framework of specific function spaces. We demonstrate that these equations possess a single global solution when specific spatial and temporal regularity conditions are satisfied. Furthermore, we show that a certain initial value problem for the time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations possesses a long-term stable solution under specific initial regularity conditions, which are optimal in nature. Notably, our approach does not rely on specific properties unique to five-dimensional spaces.

We've developed a theoretical framework for modeling spin-wave excitations within a square lattice antiferromagnet that's subject to both magnetic impurities and thermal magnon interactions. By expanding upon the spin-wave theory, we've developed a self-consistent method for calculating temperature-dependent changes in magnon bands, including bandgap widening and emerging thermal resonance modes. Furthermore, we've developed a technique for describing magnon-magnon and magnon-impurity interactions in the self-consistent scattering theory, which we used to study how magnetic impurities influence the magnon dispersion and propagate spin waves. Our theoretical model was then applied to the antiferromagnet MnF2 doped with non-magnetic impurities, with results that were compared to experimental magnon spectra obtained through neutron scattering.

The quantum encryption scheme, specifically the BB84 protocol, relies on a key preparation stage, which restricts its practicality. Utilizing a quantum computer, we can eliminate this stage by directly decoding messages in quantum form and encode them into ciphertexts without any modifications. To address potential vulnerabilities, we've adapted BB84 to use ciphertexts in the form of quantum eraser experiments, which can be measured in a ciphertext stage. We've developed two versions of the quantum eraser experiment, both of which can be implemented on current quantum computers. These modifications reduce the public-key size by half and increase the information transfer rate, although they introduce challenges in transmitting quantum states over long distances. We've proposed two potential solutions to this issue.

The effectiveness of language models is heavily reliant on their ability to predict the next word in a sentence. Given the significantly larger number of word types than tokens in most languages, most rare words are encountered only a handful of times. This paper demonstrates that existing language models can more effectively utilize information about word frequency by representing rare words through a combination of frequent base words and their respective part-of-speech tags. We introduce a novel POS-rare word replacement method, which outperforms existing rare word masking techniques in tasks such as next-word prediction, filling in missing tokens, and machine translation.
