This research aims to refine the constraints on fast radio burst (FRB) emission models through simultaneous optical and X-ray observations of the FRB source MAXI J2009.0+27. Although initially discovered in 2018 by MAXI, extensive observations have been conducted using various optical telescopes since 2021, revealing a 10 magnitude dim non-thermal counterpart. Fractals have been employed to analyze the optical light curve, revealing similarities to X-ray bursts in recurrence times and flux. This similarity in flux and temporal characteristics suggests that the optical emission may originate from the X-ray emitting region. Furthermore, integrating optical observations into existing FRB emission models could enhance our understanding of magnetar emission, particularly in the optical to X-ray transition region, and may also support models involving external shock emission, particularly in young neutron stars.

The theoretical understanding of CPA and NLO-based laser systems' performance is
poorly developed compared to experimental research, calling for improved modeling
capabilities. Establishing a reliable simulation model for NLO systems is
especially challenging due to the complex interaction between multiple physical
factors. To address this issue, a new approach is proposed that combines noise
perturbation and matrix factorization techniques to model how the nonlinear
contribution enters the laser system and develops over time. The newly created
stochastic laser equations accurately represent nanosecond laser operation and
are validated against experimental data from nanosecond oscillators, amplifiers,
and lasers that produce harmonics.

This paper introduces a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework called MAGIC, where generated text is evaluated by two evaluators: a human context coach who assesses text coherence with prior discourse, and an image evaluator who measures text's connection to an image. Through self-play, the generated text is reinforced to remain consistent with both the context and the image, without explicit coherence training. An unsupervised context coach is designed to prioritize coherence text at play, leveraging an e.g.c.r. function to quantify text's distance from the optimal coherence region based on image content. Our MAGIC framework demonstrates superior performance in the COIN dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art models in coherence-context relevance and image-text relevance metrics.

A new Delegated RingCT signature scheme is presented to enhance privacy in cryptocurrency systems like Cardano, which utilizes a Delegated Proof of Stake consensus mechanism for scalability and efficiency. The Delegated RingCT scheme allows for efficient verification, speeding up transaction processing by 10 times compared to traditional RingCT signatures, while maintaining constant processing time regardless of the number of hidden transaction amounts included.

Detailed measurements of the closed orbit deviations between beams in Super Proton Synchroton (SPS) electron-lens interaction regions have enabled a direct measurement of electron-beam impact effects that cannot be simulated without considering the actual impact. These differences were measured at frequencies up to 10 MHz, allowing for a spatial resolution of approximately 1 mm at the point of interaction between beams. Additionally, a new phenomenon known as "electron-lens feedback instability" was discovered, which occurs when the electron beam interacts with the radio-frequency feedback system present in the SPS.

Machine learning has gained significant attention in solid mechanics, particularly for calibrating parameters and solving boundary value problems. However, standard neural networks struggle with learning problems where past data influences current behavior, as is common in constitutive laws. To address this, a proposed real-time continual learning approach leverages tensor products to create and maintain a sequential network of weights that can adapt to changing material properties over time. By using online learning algorithms, this method efficiently processes an expanding dataset while avoiding the need to discard previous data. Experimental results on various problems, including various machine learning methods applied to characterizing metal and concrete materials, as well as real-time plasticity in metal materials, demonstrate the proposed method's potential in real-world applications.

A recent study of the pi+ pi0 gamma decay from J/psi decays has led to a new interpretation of the epsilon(10753) resonance, which can be described as a 1S 0^- state, in line with conventional bottomonium theory. The paper that follows examines the world-wide catalogue of omega decays, which are a mode of decay for epsilon(10753), and finds that they are under-documented, particularly omega three p pi decays, which are consistent with being 1st order in the epsilon decay sequence.

This paper showcases the benefits of combining stochastic gradient descent with askew sampling and low-precision arithmetic. We integrate askew sampling with quantized SGD to accelerate training of quantized neural networks. Our experiments reveal that AskewSGD achieves similar results in fewer iterations compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, the performance of AskewSGD is comparable to state-of-the-art reparameterized quantized SGD.

As robots become increasingly soft, they are starting to resemble the physical structures of both insect and animal limbs. Invertebrates use their soft bodies for movement, while vertebrates have evolved stiffer structures to support their increased skeletal systems. Drawing inspiration from these natural forms, researchers are now developing soft robots with reinforced structures. In a recent study, soft robot designers reported that incorporating internal structures into their designs led to noticeable improvements in performance. In this research, we examine the effects of internal structures on robot performance by employing computational models to analyze movement patterns in particles on both invertebrate and vertebrate robots. Our results indicate that invertebrate robots are more efficient and resilient, whereas vertebrate robots exhibit increased resistance to external forces. Interestingly, soft robot designers favor the internal structures of invertebrates over those of vertebrates, as evidenced by existing designs.

The Jacobi group, which is a semi-direct product of Siegel-Jacobi group $Sp(n,\mathbb{R})\ltimes T^n$ and the special unitary group $U(n)$, serves as a principal $U(n)$-bundle for the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane. A left-invariant metric on the Jacobi group is constructed and demonstrated to be equivalent to a Kähler balanced metric on the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane. Moreover, the derived left-invariant 2-form is shown to be proportional to the co-Kähler form associated with the Kähler balanced metric, and it is also identified as a left-invariant horizontal Kaluza-Klein form resulting from a specific Kaluza-Nakamura connection on the Jacobi group.

Recent advances in fact-checking have been driven by the application of deep learning techniques to claim analysis. However, existing methods face challenges in accurately processing complex statements, as they struggle to process the full text of the claim. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative approach that breaks down complex statements into simpler parts and reconstructs the fact to enhance verification accuracy. By utilizing a neural network to decompose a claim and applying a dual encoder to validate it, we can effectively process the newly generated components. Our system also incorporates a verification model with a feedback loop to refine the decomposition and improve overall performance. This method has been tested on MAFIA, the FactCheck.org dataset, and XFact datasets, where it has outperformed state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy.

This study presents an innovative generative model that produces data from a latent representation, addressing two main drawbacks of existing generative models: the need for extensive human-annotated data and overly simplistic data patterns. The proposed model is built upon a new framework that integrates two key components: the structure of existing data and the underlying relationships within the data. The human element plays a crucial role in enhancing the model by providing critical insights and guidance, resulting in a significant improvement in the quality of the generated data. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its application to image, audio, and protein image generation tasks, yielding notable results in each domain.

We've created simplified versions of hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling that replace the need for costly matrix inversions with efficient matrix multiplication. These adaptations, particularly useful for probabilistic problems represented by linear Gaussian models, replace the sampling step in slice sampling with hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling. Compared to previous methods, our new algorithms demonstrate comparable performance but significantly reduce computation time by a factor of 50 to 1000 times.

This study focuses on introducing and analyzing a novel problem, specifically designing algorithms that can efficiently handle broken paths in graphs by replacing them with new routes. To achieve this, we develop and implement algorithms that utilize fault-tolerant shortcuts to estimate the optimal path between any two vertices in the presence of failures. Our solutions, implemented in both static and dynamic settings, showcase improved performance in terms of running time and stretch. Our primary contributions include developing efficient algorithms for various types of graphs, such as unweighted graphs, weighted graphs, and those subject to edge and vertex failures. Our time and stretch complexities are improved in all cases, making our algorithms a valuable resource for network routing.

In a one-dimensional driven Bose-Hubbard model with dissipation, a continuous phase transition occurs. By computing the Fourier transforms of one- and two-particle correlations within the dissipative steady state and examining their behavior near the transition point, their relationships were determined. These correlations can be effectively described using the scaling behavior associated with the dissipative phase transition. Furthermore, the accuracy of this scaling description depends on system size and system-bath coupling strength. Notably, the scale of momentum in the scaling description is influenced by system size and system-bath coupling strength in a manner similar to the momentum scale of the non-equilibrium physics.

Let $u$ be a bounded solution to the Dirichlet problem for linear elliptic equations within a $C^{1,1}$ uniform domain. It can be demonstrated that there exists a harmonic function defined on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose non-trivial support coincides with the Dirichlet solution $\omega$ inside the domain $D$, and whose vanishing boundary coincides with $\partial D$, provided that the boundary condition $\omega$ satisfies a linear equation in $D$. Furthermore, the Dirichlet solution $\omega$ is Lipschitz continuous within any compact subset of $D$, and this property is shown to be equivalent to the non-tangential maximal function of a harmonic function being in $L^{\infty}(D,d\sigma)$.

A novel and efficient framework is presented in this research, designed to accurately segment brain tissues and identify lesions in MRI scans. To enhance accuracy, proposed modifications to existing active contour models incorporate adjustments to the statistical properties of MRI tissue data using Gaussian Processes. By redefining the energy function of Active Contour models to include an additional term derived from covariance matrices of MRI tissue types, our approach achieves improved tissue segmentation. By effectively capturing MRI tissue correlations, the resulting models produce accurate boundary detection for tumors and other lesions. Experimental findings confirm that our approach significantly improves performance compared to existing active contour methods, particularly in terms of convergence speed and accuracy.

A weakly interacting one-dimensional 1D Bose gas in a periodic driving field is examined under dissipative 1D Bose condensation conditions. Utilizing the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equation, the effects of dissipation, heating, and nonlinearity are analyzed. Interference between dissipation and field-driven heating determines condensation, while nonlinearity primarily affects the condensation rate. Notably, a nonlinearity-induced phase transition from heating to cooling, leading to condensation, is discovered. Additionally, a heating rate oscillation and its link to particle number oscillation are found. Furthermore, a heating rate decay and condensation onset in the long-time limit are found, with phase transitions in heating rate decay linked to changes in effective mass.

We examine whether highly regular sublinear functions can be expressed as convex functions with a specific level of smoothness, given certain regularity in their derivatives, and we show that this holds true if the derivative's exponent $p$ is greater than $1$ but fails when $p$ is less than $1$ by constructing a counterexample in three or more dimensions.

For acoustics and cold atoms acclimatisation, precise timing is essential, driving the demand for highly accurate and reliable timing devices. Current high-end products are extremely costly and fragile, prompting the creation of compact, affordable alternatives, such as fiber optic network-based clocks. A more recent innovation, the optical clock, has now become available, offering exceptional accuracy. However, its small size and resilience to external factors are still lacking. A key challenge lies in the role of photodetection, which is necessary for optical clocks to operate but can also introduce limitations. To address this, the authors studied the impact of photodetection on the accuracy and stability of optical clocks, using the three-level Ramsey model. Their findings suggest that Ramsey-based clocks may not be the optimal design, and alternative clock types, such as the clockless type and optical lattice clocks with fewer atoms, could potentially offer better performance.

Energy efficiency in communication networks is a pressing concern, and this study introduces a novel algorithm, HFES, to enhance the energy consumption of network paths while ensuring fault tolerance. This new approach outperforms the existing FEES algorithm in terms of energy consumption, especially under varying traffic conditions.

Recent advancements in deep metric learning have led to significant improvements in image retrieval performance. Despite these advancements, a fundamental challenge persists: a model may inadvertently capture irrelevant information that hinders its ability to distinguish between unique features of different images. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Gradient Descent Learning (GDL) that integrates a regularization technique to mitigate the adverse effect. The method exploits the fact that the gradient of a pair-wise loss can be decomposed into components that either contribute positively or negatively to retrieval performance. By analyzing the composition of the gradient, L2 regularization can be effectively applied to filter out the detrimental parts, thereby improving retrieval performance. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of GD learning on a variety of pair-wise losses and a significant improvement in retrieval results.

We examine the inherent structural limitations imposed by error correction codes constructed from an exclusive set of tensors arranged in a tensor network format. We prove that if a tensor network represents an erasure correction code using only one type of tensor, it is restricted to one dimension, essentially forming a code similar to the Reed-Muller code. Furthermore, if a tensor network represents a quantum LDPC code using two distinct tensor types, it is also confined to one dimension. In contrast, we develop a method to create infinite families of tensor network-based erasure codes with linear distance, linear number of physical qubits, and a constant ratio of the two for any spatial dimension above one. We also establish a connection to tensor networks representing classical erasure codes, demonstrating the existence of an infinite family with linear distance, polynomial total length, and a constant ratio of the two, where the total length represents the total number of classical tensors used.

The origin of magnetized radio filaments in star-forming galaxies is still unclear.
Our research suggests two possible explanations for the formation of these radio filaments:
a) they are a natural result of the gravitational collapse of magnetized gas, or
b) they are created by colliding gas streams.
To investigate this, we developed a new simulation tool that simulates the behavior of these radio filaments.
Our tool was tested by analyzing radio filaments in the galaxy NGC 1068, and the results showed that both formation mechanisms can explain the observed properties of these radio filaments.
This has implications for understanding the large-scale structure of galaxies and the role of magnetic fields in star formation.

Controlling large groups of distributed energy resources with multiple inputs and outputs poses a significant challenge. To address this, numerous leader-follower-based methods have been proposed, allowing a centralized controller to dictate the desired behavior while individual resources follow. This paper examines the control of inverters that can adjust both active power and voltage, aiming to control the power output at specific points of interconnection with the grid, known as point of common coupling. The central controller sends desired values for active power and voltage magnitude to each inverter, instructing the resources to track these values. The control strategy for the resources is designed to ensure stability and achieve the specified power output, even in cases where multiple resources are connected to the same bus. This approach allows for the allocation of power sharing constraints, even in cases where there are unequal numbers of controllers and points of common coupling. The control strategy is shown to converge asymptotically, even in cases where there are multiple controllers influencing a single bus. The results of the research demonstrate that this control strategy enables a stable and scalable power grid, even in cases where there are numerous controllers and distributed resources interacting with traditional grids or with high penetration levels of renewable energy sources.

This research presents a regret bound for a non-stationary multi-armed bandit problem with geometrically deteriorating and delaying performance in its optimal option. The researcher relies on a unique method that transforms data from varying distributions into a unified framework, allowing a nearly optimal, time-varying regret limit to be reached. Unlike other researchers who focus on regret bounds influenced by shifts in the mean or reward patterns, this work highlights the significance of loss and delay rates of the most beneficial arm. The findings demonstrate that a rate of logarithmic growth can be avoided if the loss rate is at least 1, whereas it is only guaranteed if the delay rate is at least 1. The study also incorporates a technique that utilizes information about delay times to tailor an algorithm that achieves the desired regret limit, whereas a blind algorithm that disregards delay times only achieves a suboptilinear, yet poorer, regret limit.

We present a text-generation framework for dialogue that leverages prior dialogue history and is built on a problem-solving foundation. This problem-based approach offers a text-generation model that surpasses the current state-of-the-art in both efficiency and analysis. Firstly, it enables the development of dialogue systems with the ability to break down dialogue goals into smaller sub-goals, thus enhancing goal-oriented dialogue systems. Secondly, it provides a text-generation model with a better understanding of dialogue goals and effective resource allocation. Thirdly, it allows for the design of highly efficient text-generation systems by leveraging history to predict subsequent dialogue turns. Lastly, it offers a text-generation model with the ability to naturally incorporate dialogue goals and assess success within the context of the overall dialogue.

Quantum chromodynamics, formulated in the 1960s, has been a cornerstone of understanding the strong interactions between subatomic particles. Over the decades, particularly the last 30 years, QCD has been a fertile ground for theoretical and experimental exploration. Initially, researchers focused on whether quarks and gluons could be isolated, but the answer was quickly established as negative. Subsequently, the focus shifted to examining the characteristics of strong-interaction matter in various conditions, driven by advancements in both theoretical frameworks and experimental capabilities.

The variability of operational loads on offshore wind turbines is heavily influenced by the stochastic nature of wind turbulence and the irregular waves that they encounter in their environment. To address this, we've developed a novel method for quantifying the dispersion of loads on offshore wind turbines, which we've then applied to a specific turbine model located offshore from the European offshore wind laboratory. Our investigation has revealed significant differences in load dispersion under different environmental conditions, specifically when exposed to extreme wind events versus when subjected to regular wave motions. Furthermore, we've discovered that the presence of additional wave motions tends to amplify the variability of load distributions, leading to increased peak load occurrences. Our findings also suggest that the stochastic nature of individual load measures may necessitate the use of probabilistic limit states, rather than solely relying on mean-based limit states.

This research aims to explore the connection between Twitter sentiment and
phenomena triggered by natural disasters, such as secondary events and impacts,
utilizing social media data and Twitter's vast network of users. By leveraging
social media, we can capture public sentiment and real-time reactions, making
it a valuable resource for tracking the changes occurring after disasters.
To achieve this goal, we will apply NLP techniques to analyze the public's
emotional responses expressed on Twitter, enabling us to map sentiment across
time and space, and identify any subsequent events or impacts. We will
demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to multiple
disasters, starting with an examination of the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake
and Tsunami.

We prove that the absolute nilpotency degree of a group with a normal subgroup of prime order p divides the order of p if the group exhibits R-nilpotency of degree k. It follows that the absolute nilpotency degree of a group with a normal subgroup of order p replaces the order of p with a prime number r in the notation p^r, where r is less than or equal to k. We also investigate the cases where k is three or four.

A new approach to deconvolving spectroscopic data is developed, allowing for the accurate reconstruction of individual molecular responses in ultrafast spectroscopy. This data-driven technique can be applied without prior knowledge of the responding species. By considering the effects of noise in experimental data, the method is demonstrated using coherent Raman spectroscopy. It is shown that molecular populations can be precisely extracted, even when the data is noisy. This has significant implications for studying complex molecular systems.

This study presents a statistical framework for tracking objects in virtual scenes within driving environments, incorporating factors such as object visibility, occlusion, and transient presence. We present this model through a detailed analysis of a virtual driving scenario featuring an obstructed object. The proposed framework, Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA), associates potential scenarios with measurement conditions and assigns probabilities to each, ensuring only the most likely associations influence tracking performance. The results obtained from our JPDA model demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately tracking objects within virtual driving scenarios.

In this research, we have developed a model for reflected entropy within the framework of interface conformal field theory, specifically in three dimensions. Utilizing the operator algebra approach, we've found that in specific scenarios, the reflected entropy exhibits universal characteristics, such as the Markov gap. Furthermore, we've found that when considering the presence of a domain wall, the reflected entropy can be expressed through the central charges k_1 and k_2, which are unique to theory describing the domain wall's behavior. Our findings also show that the reflected entropy is unaffected by the specific boundary conditions applied to the theory.

In this research, we apply an enhanced version of the extreme learning machine (ELM) for channel estimation in systems with limited cyclic prefix length and hardware inaccuracies, leveraging the sparse nature of the channel. The invariance of ELM's learning phase to weight matrix changes allows it to be a suitable choice for channel estimation. However, the conventional ELM is limited by its sensitivity to the design matrix, prompting us to develop an ELM variant that relies on an orthogonal matrix, thereby reducing sensitivity to input data conditions. We analyze the least squares solution of the ELM with orthogonal matrix and confirm that the matrix's orthogonality ensures a stable solution, making it less dependent on the size and characteristics of the design matrix. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed ELM with orthogonal matrix achieves better performance compared to conventional methods, including ELM and OSA, especially in scenarios with imperfect hardware.

In the context of quantum mechanics, it is often assumed that measurements are exclusively projective. However, we aim to demonstrate that projective measurement outcomes can also be achieved using non-projective, yet commuting measurements. Specifically, we will show that the density matrix eigenvalues obtained from non-projective measurements on subsystems of entangled states can mimic those from projective measurements, even when entanglement does not adhere to a specific 'criteria'. Consequently, this suggests that the application of the reduced density matrix method to entanglement analysis is more widespread than previously thought. Our approach involves a novel way of categorizing entangled states and has significant implications for entanglement research.

G2-instantons exhibit a degree of stability, meaning they are only slightly affected by certain distortions. This property led us to investigate the boundary of the space of abelian instantons, revealing that they fall into distinct categories based on their topology. Furthermore, we demonstrated that instantons within a single topological class cannot continuously transform into those of a different topological class, implying a level of rigidity. This rigor also applies to non-abelian instantons, where we found that the moduli space of fixed non-abelian configurations is compact.

Despite the significant potential of contact tracing technology, its use poses risks of government-led mass surveillance due to the underlying principles of data collection and tracking. To mitigate these concerns, data providers must ensure the privacy of contact tracing data, especially when using location-based datasets. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of creating such data while preserving the privacy of individuals involved, by developing a new method for generating artificial contact traces without compromising individual locations. This technique, known as 'differential private splicing', allows us to create contact traces that are distinct from real locations, yet preserve essential data such as the number of contacts and the overall density of the contact network. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments using New York City data, showing that our method can produce realistic contact traces that are indistinguishable from actual data, while ensuring the privacy of individuals involved.

A new approach to understanding entanglement in interaction-free entanglement (IFE) is presented, which involves introducing a method to analyze the role of decoherence in the entanglement process. Our method, based on the application of interaction terms to a decohered system, enables the investigation of how decoherence impacts IFE and how subsequent interaction and entanglement occur. Our results show that a combination of the inverse decoherence process and a weak measurement process are both necessary to achieve successful IFE. Our proposed approach offers a novel way to understand the combined effects of decoherence, the Zeno effect, and the interaction-free measurement process, and sheds light on how entanglement arises in this context.

We've developed a method for producing verifiable compiler output by requiring that the generated code match a precise specification. This is achieved by considering the compiler as a translator of abstract concepts into another form, enabling us to establish rigorous proofs of its effectiveness. Focusing on a specific type of translator - one that converts Hoare logic assertions from one language to another - we've demonstrated the feasibility of this approach by applying it to the CompCert x86 compiler, which is certified in Coq, for x86-64 architecture. By establishing the CompCert compiler as a translator of precise logic assertions from x86-64 to x86, we've provided a novel verification technique that can be used to confirm the compiler's correctness, in addition to existing verification methods.

Recent research has uncovered a potential member of the genus Iochroma in the Peruvian Peruvian-Chilean border region. The discovery is being further verified by the publication of the species' first DNA sequence.

This extension of Ramanujan's well-known identity utilizing the Hurwitz zeta function can be derived from a kernel of the zeta function itself, ultimately related to Bernoulli polynomials and their properties as an alternating zeta function.

We introduce the concept of $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory when $T$ is a 2-dimensional torus and $E$ is a specific type of elliptic curve with complex multiplication, the curve's automorphism group is the same as the curve's complex numbers. Our work is the first in its field to address the challenges presented by the additional variable resulting from the curve. To tackle the associated problems, we use methods developed by Hopkins and Kuhn, the Kac-Vakhtin formulas, and a unique characteristic map that arises from the curve's variable. The construction is the first of its kind in the context of commutative ring spectra. Our work also includes an in-depth analysis of the associated homology theory, which has significant applications in algebraic geometry.

Discovering and utilizing geometric data structures is a key aspect of unsupervised learning. By examining the underlying structure of data, we can gain deeper insights into its organization. The concept of geometric data structures has been widely used in various fields such as clustering, dimensionality reduction, and manifold learning. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of new methods that leverage both local and global geometric information. These methods have been applied to complex data structures, such as point clouds, and have shown promising results. In particular, deep learning-based approaches have been developed that combine different types of information, and have been applied to various tasks, such as classification and clustering. These methods have been shown to outperform traditional techniques in terms of performance and scalability.

Our research examines the creation of charmonium pairs through a different process than the one that dominates at a few GeV. This alternative process, known as two-gluon fusion, is possible when the center-of-mass energy is above 10 GeV. We've calculated the differential cross-section for the production of heavy quarkonium pairs through two-gluon fusion. Our analysis focused specifically on the productions of $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ combinations. Utilizing relativistic QCD, we've determined the next-to-leading order contributions. Our results show that the production of $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ combinations are more sensitive to the behavior of the charm quark at low momentum than the productions of $J/\psi + \chi_{c1}$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{c2}$. Furthermore, by comparing with experimental data from a collider, we found that the productions of $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ provide a more accurate indication of the charm quark's behavior than the productions of $J/\psi + \chi_{c1}$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{c2}$.

As a secure and widely-used messaging platform, Signal relies on each user's personal 6-digit  PIN to protect their account.  Despite its popularity, there is a lack of research on how users from diverse backgrounds approach their Signal PINs. To bridge this knowledge gap, our study investigates how users select and manage their Signal PINs. A comprehensive online survey was conducted, resulting in 1,002 completed responses. The study's key findings include: users' level of awareness about their PIN's function impacts their complexity; some users reuse their Signal PINs across multiple devices; and approximately 10% of users report storing their PINs in a physical notebook. The study's outcomes can inform the development of more effective security measures for Signal and other messaging platforms.

In certain situations, precise calculations of solar energy over the sphere require a quadrature rule with low node count that accurately reflects the solar irradiance, which varies inversely with the square of the distance from the sun to the surface. Traditional spherical quadrature rules, designed for uniform distribution, may introduce unnecessary inaccuracies in this context. Here, an alternative quasilattice rule is proposed, based on the Cuckoo's Hash Lattice, which offers a stable and efficient alternative by providing a fixed shift that ensures consistent results for any solar angle. The proposed rule achieves high precision in calculations near the center of the sphere, with minimal loss of precision even at the edges, and requires fewer nodes than traditional rules for calculations within five degrees of the sun's position, with only a 1% error compared to the theoretical radiation value.

In deep learning, the key challenge is to identify the optimal model parameters that minimize error. The optimal direction for parameter adjustment is determined by the gradient vector, whose magnitude is influenced by eigenvalues associated with the direction of the steepest ascent. The first derivative of the loss function is typically computed using backpropagation, but the second derivative is computationally expensive to calculate using automatic differentiation. We introduce ViViT, a variational vector-tensor estimator, which efficiently approximates both the eigenvalues and directional derivatives of specific derivative tensors. ViViT learns a function that maps a given matrix to a set of eigenvalues, achieving a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy. The proposed approach is applied to second-order optimization methods, such as L-BFGS, to accelerate neural network training.

This study delves into how language models with word embeddings that contain gender-based biases can perpetuate unfair treatment in AI-driven systems. We examine how addressing this bias, without compromising linguistic accuracy, affects word embeddings in French, German, and Spanish across three distinct data sources. We discovered a link between removing gender-based biases and changes in the embeddings' quality, which are strongly influenced by the language's grammatical structure. We also discovered that embedding quality can be maintained by adjusting the order of training, which involves first stripping away biases, then incorporating linguistic details, and finally, fine-tuning the model.

A finitely generated virtually nilpotent group can be viewed as the quotient of a nilpotent group by a finite one, and its action on a specific space differs significantly from the nilpotent case due to a non-trivial, non-abelian quotient.  We demonstrate that this non-trivial quotient has a profound impact on dynamics, specifically showing that the resulting dynamics under these actions is chaotic in nature, and further, that the set of characters that are stable under the action is both non-trivial and unique in character, exhibiting a characteristic "fractal" pattern.

This paper presents a novel approach to obtaining accurate three-dimensional pose estimates from position and orientation data through optimization techniques. A key component of the approach involves developing a novel loss function to optimize estimated three-dimensional poses. Experimental results show that the approach can increase the accuracy of three-dimensional pose estimates by up to 10% compared to a baseline method. Furthermore, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated with other network architectures to enhance pose estimation precision.

This study focuses on developing a high-performance, low-latency, and generalizable model for predicting travel time in urban environments. Building upon the success of gradient boosting decision trees, a novel framework, GBM4traffic, is proposed, which leverages historical traffic data and road network information. The GBM4traffic model achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming graph neural networks by at least 1.5% in terms of accuracy, while also demonstrating superior generalizability and performance across diverse cities. The research highlights the potential of using non-spatial methods in addressing complex mobility challenges.

Causal inference techniques are increasingly being utilized in machine learning research, particularly in addressing fairness issues in classification problems. New causal inference methods can now provide a clear evaluation of counterfactual fairness. However, this evaluation is hindered by the absence of a clear causal model, which poses a significant challenge in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, a new approach has been developed that uses a variational autoencoder to create a causal model from a given dataset. This approach allows for the evaluation of counterfactual fairness. Experimental results have demonstrated that this method can effectively identify cases where fairness cannot be achieved. Furthermore, a new method has been developed to address fairness issues by leveraging a non-convex optimization problem. This approach can be used in both linear and non-linear settings. Experimental results have shown that this method can effectively improve fairness without compromising model accuracy.

The upcoming generation of radio telescopes, such as the MWA and SKA, will generate vast amounts of data, necessitating an ability to process it locally due to the immense data rates involved. This substantial data volume hampers the ability to achieve the desired sensitivity if data is transmitted at high rates. To overcome this challenge, we have developed a new, distributed system for managing radio telescope data processing, dubbed DiSKa. DiSKa enables the distribution of tasks across multiple locations and facilitates the efficient handling of large data sets by splitting sensitive data across local storage. In this paper, we delve into the underlying principles of DiSKa and examine its potential applications within the context of large radio telescope arrays.

A cutting-edge field called metaphotonics is rapidly gaining momentum, leveraging optically-manipulated photon fields to manipulate light and produce innovative effects not easily achievable through conventional optically-induced methods. In this study, we introduce a novel method to magnetically excite a photon field via an optically-induced artificial magnetic resonance that exploits spatially and temporally non-reciprocal interactions between the light and the electrons. The proposed method relies on an inhomogeneous interaction between light and electrons that varies across the light wavefront. The inhomogeneous interaction causes the light's electric field to twist into a complex, two-dimensional polarization state that we refer to as optical magnetic polarization. When driven by this optical magnetic polarization, the electrons absorb energy from the light and enter a non-local, time-derivative interaction that generates a magnetic dipole moment. The interaction between the optical magnetic resonances and the light results in new optical phenomena, such as magnetic Faraday rotation and the Purcell effect, that are distinct from those of topological photonics and conventional topological photonics.

We have developed a novel approach to assessing an actor's star power based on their ability to forecast a movie's anticipated earnings. This concept relies on predicting the revenue a film will generate from ticket sales, a task that involves analyzing various aspects of the movie, such as its production details, reviews, and the actors' reputations. Our method focuses on predicting a film's revenue in two distinct geographical areas: worldwide and by country. By applying this concept to quantify star power, we have identified correlations between a movie's global revenue and its director's previous work, as well as the countries where the movie was produced. Additionally, we have found significant relationships between a movie's country-by-country revenue and factors such as the country where the director's career began, the actors' countries of origin, and the reviews the movie received.

This paper employs a rigorous mathematical framework, incorporating continuous and discrete variable models, to analyze the stability of low-frequency voltage in power grids. Utilizing established models for power system dynamics, including steady-state, primary frequency, secondary frequency, and quasi-static voltage control, we derive a reduced-order model that can be analyzed through two different approaches, both of which involve second-order systems. Our method allows us to examine how secondary frequency control, a crucial component in networks with high inelastic loads, influences the dynamics of frequency and voltage, and ultimately, how these effects can be analyzed using a simpler model.

This paper examines cyber-physical systems, which integrate two distinct layers of design: a connection network and a system that operates outside of that network. The system outside of the connection network is controlled by feedback and can be non-linear in nature. The connection network uses a connection protocol that exchanges control data between its connected nodes. The primary objective of this paper is to develop an assessment method for network layers that exchange control data between their connected nodes. The evaluation method should be applicable to systems with non-linear models and outside of connection network feedback control. The proposed approach involves defining network performance in relation to system outside of connection network performance and network robustness. Network performance is measured using the concept of robust decoupling in non-linear systems. The concept of network robustness is introduced to quantify network performance. The proposed approach is demonstrated through an example of a system controlled by a PID network.

Blazars, a type of active galactic nucleus, emit intense radiation in the UV and X-ray spectra, and studying their polarization could provide insight into their complex astrophysical surroundings. Research has been conducted on MCG 0231+349, a blazar that experienced an increase in UV and X-ray radiation between 2015 and 2017, to determine its polarization. By analyzing the data, scientists have found that the polarization of light from this blazar is likely due to the interaction of multiple emission components. Although initial findings suggest that the polarization is primarily due to the synchrotron radiation of the dominant emission component, further study and modeling are needed to fully understand the behavior of these emission components.

The properties of hessian matrices are examined in both replica-symmetric and
replica-symmetry-broken spin glass landscapes, considering techniques such as
one-step and many-step replica-symmetry breaking, as well as thermal interpolation
methods. Our key finding indicates that the thermal representation accurately
reflects the landscape's replica-symmetry breaking structure, unlike one-step
breaching, but unlike many-step breaching which introduces irrelevant modes.
The research also shows that, unlike many-body systems, the Hessian spectrum
is insensitive to the type of replica-symmetry-breaking, except in marginal cases.
Furthermore, our analysis shows that replica-space hessians are unitary equivalent
to physical-space hessians, suggesting that hessian-based methods, such as
dimensionality reduction, are applicable to glassy systems.

In the context of online learning, our research focuses on identifying multiple symmetric states that share a consistent level of similarity. We developed performance metrics for sequential online methods, which were also applied to offline scenarios. These results indicate that most online methods are effective when the level of similarity between the states is a constant, a finding also supported by real-world experiments. However, when it comes to a specific setup where the offline approach is suboptimal, a variant of the Hammersley-威尔逊 algorithm can surpass online methods in both online and offline settings.

A method to utilize the mass spectrum of light mesons to estimate the mass spectrum of light baryons in QCD is presented. By applying this technique to the mass differences within baryon triplets, we calculate the masses of various light baryons using an analysis of their scalar form factors. By incorporating the corresponding light meson mass spectrum, we derive the masses of light baryons with a single strange quark and those composed entirely of light flavors. Our results show that these masses align well with experimental data, demonstrating agreement with measured values to within approximately 5-10%.

The investigation of the sun's deep meridional circulation via acoustic waves is explored in this research. A recent study by Papp et al. (2021) proposed a method to measure the sun's radial and horizontal flow using acoustic wave phase speeds. This study builds on their work by analyzing how these speeds are influenced by the meridional flow and the depth at which the waves are generated. A simplified model of the sun's meridional circulation was created and used to simulate wave propagation in the sun's interior. The simulations revealed that the travel times of upward-propagating acoustic waves are significantly affected by the downflow and the depth at which the waves are generated. This sensitivity to the downflow is primarily due to the effect of the downflow on the wave phase speeds, rather than the effect of the wave group speeds. This finding is crucial for the interpretation of the sun's meridional circulation, as it suggests that the travel times of the upward-propagating acoustic waves can be used to estimate the downflow and the depth at which the waves are generated.

The presence of a magnetic field in the early universe significantly alters the behavior of gravitational waves, as its transverse components can interact with the waves and induce anisotropies in scalar perturbations. These interactions result in a propagation speed for gravitational waves that differs from the speed of light, as well as a refraction of gravitational waves due to the external magnetic field. Additionally, gravitational waves can experience a shift in their polarization states and a difference in propagation speeds between the two polarizations. These phenomena can ultimately affect the ringdown frequencies of gravitational waves, as well as their generation in the early universe, potentially leading to observable imprints in their power spectra.

The proposed Deep 4D Light Field (LF) representation method consists of two components: a disparity-aided model and a learned latent code. The LF volume is initially segmented into multiple slices, and each slice is represented by a learned 3D patch, and an allotropic filter bank to enhance detail. A neural network then generates an encoding for these patches, allowing for efficient 4D LF compression. Experimental results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in 4D LF image coding.

We introduce a semi-interactive approach to cross-lingual information retrieval, 
utilizing an online query expansion strategy to efficiently enhance retrieval 
precision. By leveraging a real-time, semantic query expansion technique, the 
method can significantly improve the retrieval results with a minimal number of 
interactive sessions. Our research demonstrates that even a single interaction 
can yield a notable enhancement in retrieval accuracy. Furthermore, a few 
sessions involving three or four iterations can further significantly 
maximize the retrieval effectiveness.

This research introduces a new approach to tackle the challenge of inferring underlying demographic patterns from data that is subject to measurement errors. The underlying population is conceptualized as a spatially distributed set of discrete units, modeled using a Gaussian process to capture its spatial dynamics. Observations are made through a series of noisy measurements, modelled as a linear combination of the population units and a random error. The model's parameters are estimated using a combination of a prior distribution and a loss function that balances the trade-off between accuracy and smoothness. The results of our study demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in a simulated study, showcasing its ability to recover the underlying population density and make reliable predictions.

A comprehensive quantum model of memory gambling is presented, incorporating both horizontal and vertical quantum components. The strategy for maximizing returns in this context is identified and explained using a simple example of a two-qubit system. The analysis also includes an examination of the conditions under which entanglement occurs within the gambling model, with particular attention paid to the role of partial measurements. The conditions under which partial measurements can result in entanglement are identified and a relationship between the probability of such outcomes and the von Neumann entropy is established. The conditions under which a gambling strategy can lead to a guaranteed profit are also determined.

We compared the results of calculations for the band band gap and density of states of GaAs, based on the ground-state structure, using the GW method with two different initial structure estimates. Our analysis shows that GW calculations are sensitive to the initial ground-state structure, but this can be mitigated through numerical adjustments. When compared to the same GW calculations, but using different methods to obtain initial potential, our results indicate that the accuracy of GW calculations can be significantly improved by employing more accurate ground-state estimates.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider searches for the rare decay of $\Sigma^+$ particles into a proton and a $\mu^-$ and muon antineutrino using data collected in 2015. In proton-proton collisions, $\Sigma^+$ particles are generated and can be identified through their distinctive two-track signatures in the detector. By applying a multivariate analysis to track candidates, a statistical excess was found at 2.3 standard deviations, consistent with the predicted rare decay of $\Sigma^+$ particles. Additionally, upper limits on the rare decay branching fraction were calculated for different scenarios, ranging from 0.01% to 0.07% with varying assumptions about background noise.

A protoplanetary disk's mid-plane and upper layers exhibit distinct characteristics, driven by the weak vertical mixing of dust and heat. This paper investigates a model where turbulent intensity varies according to the epicyclic frequency, resulting in reduced turbulence at lower altitudes. This variation can be attributed to a weak magnetic field or shear turbulence, and it's shown that the mid-plane remains isolated from turbulent activity in the disk's upper layers. This mechanism can also be applied to angular momentum transport in accretion disks.

We have developed a method to determine the optimal atmospheric dispersion corrector design by evaluating the performance of various models, using the GAIA2 spectrograph as a case study. We have identified that the CHARLES model offers a more accurate representation of atmospheric dispersion in the blue spectrum compared to others, and we have shown that a single corrector can effectively cover the full field of view of the GAIA2 spectrograph. We have also found that a corrector designed with the ATCDM2011 model can cause image shifts of up to 0.2 pixels, which can be corrected by adjusting the telescope mirror.

The conventional practice of using Gaussian process regression with Gaussian noise often fails to accurately capture complex patterns in input variables, which is particularly problematic in real-world scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a more effective model by integrating a Bayesian neural network (BNN) with the Horseshoe prior (SH) into Gaussian process regression. This integration, known as BNN-GP with Horseshoe prior, enables a more detailed representation of input variables and significantly enhances the model's predictive capabilities. By decoupling BNN and GP, we can leverage the strengths of both models while maintaining computational efficiency. To estimate the model's hyperparameters, we've employed the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method within No-U-Turn Sampling (NUTS), ensuring a robust and accurate model performance. Our experimental results demonstrate that BNN-GP with Horseshoe prior surpasses existing regression techniques in terms of both prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

Continuous logic's localized type spaces and their underlying spaces can be connected to abelian group duality, specifically to the Pontryagin duality. Connecting these type spaces to specific dual spaces allows for classification and explicit calculations to be carried out in theory. Several theories have been proven to exhibit this connection, including abelian group theory, abelian p-groups theory, theory of countable abelian p-groups and its restricted version. Additionally, abelian group theory shows a continuous equivalence to a theory involving a specific group with specific invariant subgroups.

This paper explores an end-to-end solution for training ethical machine learning models within the constraints of federated learning by introducing a novel optimization framework. The study delves into how this approach can satisfy fairness metrics, improve model performance across diverse datasets, and incorporate differential privacy to protect sensitive data. By leveraging kernel methods, the research demonstrates that training ethical models using only local data and partial privacy protections yields comparable results to a centralized training process.

A simplified dark matter model, incorporating a $Z'$ boson resonance, is studied with the goal of reconciling conflicting constraints from electric dipole moment, flavor anomalies and dark matter observations. We analyze how this model affects dark matter signals in various experiments, including direct and indirect searches, as well as resonance peaks in both hadron colliders and electron-positron colliders. Furthermore, we propose resonance-enhanced searches at the future FCC-ee and the future circular electron positron collider, which offer improved sensitivity over resonance searches at the LHC.

This study explores deep unsupervised learning as a means to automatically
identify optimal antenna configurations in wireless communication systems, where
optimization is necessary to achieve optimal performance in various scenarios.
We compare the proposed method to genetic algorithms (GAs) in numerous
scenarios, including different user and antenna counts, and in the presence of
varying levels of channel uncertainty. Our results show that the proposed
approach surpasses GAs in both performance and computational efficiency, with
a notable advantage in scalability.

To assess the strength of beta decays in neutron-rich nuclei, we employed a quasi-particle random phase approximation calculation, utilizing the Gogny interaction. By focusing on the role of nuclear configurations, we studied 12 isotopes of fluorine, selecting two distinct configurations to analyze their influence on decay strength and distribution. Our findings reveal that both the parent and daughter nuclei, as well as nuclear phase transitions, impact the characteristics of the decay strength. Additionally, we evaluated the impact of the Gogny interaction on the distribution of the decay strength.

A model of minimal dark matter with a vector dark matter candidate is presented. 
It includes a singlet scalar that influences the dark matter relic density and a 
right-handed neutrino linked to the scalar via a Yukawa coupling, enabling 
neutrinoless double beta decay. The model's influence on a variety of fields, 
including dark matter, Higgs, right-handed neutrino and right-handed quark mixing, 
is examined. It's found that under certain conditions, it can meet all relevant 
observational constraints, offering an attractive framework for dark matter and 
neutrino mass generation.

This paper introduces an innovative learning-based control strategy that integrates Gaussian Processes with a Value-Iteration algorithm to estimate costs in high-dimensional systems. By utilizing available data to learn cost functions, Gaussian Processes can fill in the gaps when data is scarce, making the approach more efficient than traditional reinforcement learning methods. A comprehensive analysis of Gaussian Process properties demonstrates the proposed method's convergence and consistency with the Value-Iteration algorithm. To validate the approach's effectiveness, we apply it to the Swing-Up task in the CartPole system, where experimental results show the proposed method outperforms standard reinforcement learning methods, particularly in scenarios with limited data.

The higher-spin currents in a free boson theory can be deformed without breaking its higher-spin Ward identities when using the Ward identity as a guide, similar to a bootstrap approach. This method naturally leads to the discovery of Ward identities for complex spin-three symmetry, which is part of the A_2 Toda conformal field theory. Although the current method doesn't directly yield the spin-three current, it does allow for its construction once a specific three-point function is identified. This method can also be applied to the case of SL(3,R) Ward identities, which are related to A_1 \otimes A_2 and \otimes B_2 Toda conformal field theories.

We assess the effectiveness of using relation networks in enhancing Generative Adversarial Networks, specifically for super-resolution and non-local image generative models. By integrating relation networks, our super-resolution architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance, and we also introduce a new super-resolution benchmark for quantitative evaluation. Furthermore, we introduce a relation network inspired alternative to conventional non-local blocks and demonstrate that the relation-guided U-Net architecture attains state-of-the-art results on the CIFAR-10 super-resolution task. We also introduce a relation-guided super-resolution model tailored for natural images. We investigate the impact of relation networks on the non-local architecture's performance, demonstrating significant improvements across multiple datasets. We introduce CIFAR-10 super-resolution as a benchmark to compare different models, and our relation-guided network attains state-of-the-art results on this benchmark. We demonstrate that relation networks enhance the non-local block's super-resolution performance on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

We present a computational model for evaluating the security of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems, specifically designed for twin-field QKD protocols. Our approach relies on a dual reference frame framework to resolve challenges related to two-time states and allows for an arbitrary global phase reference. By incorporating the complete dual basis set, we can accurately account for all possible measurement outcomes and avoid ignoring any relevant information. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, we apply it to analyze two-variable twin-field QKD protocols and compare our findings with existing security evaluations in the field.

In this study, a specific class of Toeplitz operators is considered with symbols belonging to weighted $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock spaces on the unit disk, and their compactness, continuity, and boundedness are examined when acting between these spaces, with further exploration of their commutators.

This study introduces an efficient method for transforming object detection pseudo bounding boxes into accurate labels, leveraging a combination of model predictions and fixed rules. By integrating these boxes with rules that utilize class-specific properties, such as bounding box aspect ratios, we refine pseudo labels to enhance object detector performance. To validate the proposed approach, we applied it to the task of labeling cell nuclei in a cell segmentation task. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods for object detection and cell nucleus localization, with outcomes approaching the performance of fully supervised models.

This research examines the spectral characteristics of the Serpens South star-forming area, focusing on how self-absorption affects the observed features of ionized and neutral gas. Self-absorption occurs when a warm, partially transparent medium is situated in front of a cooler, more extensive background source. In the case of the Serpens South observations, this effect is caused by a layer of gas that is much thinner than the size of the region being observed. Our data indicates that ionized gas is observed in front of a background of neutral gas, which is in contrast to the previously established model where neutral gas is situated in front of ionized gas. This discrepancy highlights the presence of a strong wind from a massive star that is responsible for pushing the ionized gas in front of the ionization front. Our findings also indicate that the ionized gas in the wind is only partially transparent to ionizing photons, which is contrary to the previously established model. This is due to the fact that the wind is not uniform and is characterized by the presence of holes and filaments. Our data also indicates that the wind is not stationary and is characterized by the presence of fluctuations in velocity and density.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to significant breakthroughs in image classification, with both Transformers and convolutional networks achieving remarkable results. These models have unique inherent characteristics that influence their performance. We've observed that both types of models tend to focus on the center of images, with this tendency being particularly pronounced in transformers. We attribute this phenomenon in transformers to the self-attention mechanism. Furthermore, it's evident that both models perform better when they focus on the center, whereas in segmentation tasks, models that pay attention to peripheral areas tend to excel. We've also discovered that while convolutional networks can scan entire images, those with a narrow field of view, like certain types of vision transformers, may struggle to process images thoroughly.

This study develops a straightforward model to forecast mortality rates. The basic model is a factor analysis with time-varying factor loadings and additive error. The model is easy to implement and efficient, even in the presence of noisy data. The model's ability to capture complex patterns in historical data is key to its success. The model is applied to UK mortality data, yielding more accurate long-term forecasts than the standard model. The model is also effective at forecasting in a challenging environment, such as a pandemic. The 2020 COVID-19 outbreak led to a significant increase in mortality rates across Europe. The excess mortality rates are highly variable, making accurate forecasting difficult. The proposed model is shown to be a valuable tool for accurate short-term forecasts in a dynamic environment. The model is applied to European mortality data and provides accurate one-year-ahead forecasts. The results indicate that incorporating time-varying factors and leveraging recent information can lead to accurate forecasts. The proposed approach is a viable option for mortality forecasting, especially in situations with limited data.

A neural architecture search method is introduced to counter the effects of interference in neural network training, which occurs when previously learned knowledge conflicts with new information. This approach utilizes earlier successful designs as starting points for the search process, effectively preventing interference and preserving beneficial characteristics. Evaluations using different datasets and models demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, showing improved performance over other architecture search methods. Specifically, performance enhancements of 1.6% and 1.5% were observed over RoBERTa and ELECTRA-based models, respectively. Moreover, retrieved architectural performance exceeded that of randomly designed models by 3.6% on the GLUE benchmark.

A time-series feature extraction packge known as `trade` has been developed to address the limitations of existing feature extraction packages, which are plagued by issues such as poor modularity, inflexibility, and scalability. The `trade` package is designed to facilitate the extraction of a broad range of time-series features, encompassing both fundamental and advanced methodologies, in a modular and flexible manner. It achieves this by allowing users to easily customize feature extraction processes, define custom features, and parallelize computations across multiple time series. Additionally, the package provides built-in functionality for anomaly detection and down-selecting relevant features based on statistical significance and mutual information scores.

We have demonstrated a geodesic completion analog of Hume's theorem, specifically, we showed that a geodesically complete CAT(0) space with a maximally elliptic fundamental group is properly quasi-isometric. This builds on previous research, including Hume's original CAT(0) space proof and later developments by Kapovich and Xu. Our proof draws inspiration from recent work by Dymarz and Wilton on completion problems for CAT(0) spaces. A key aspect of our results involves extending Hume's notion of ellipticity to groups quasi-isometric to non-complete CAT(0) spaces. Furthermore, we provide a concrete example of such a group based on Dymarz and Wilton's construction of non-geodesically complete CAT(0) squares-on-circles. In addition, we explore a related concept where geodesic completeness is substituted with quasi-properness, yielding another max-ellipticity-to-quasi-isometric-properness equivalence that mirrors Hume's theorem.

This paper outlines our methodology for analyzing the 2019 WMT Quality Assessment results. A key aspect of our approach lies in the statistical examination of translator, reviewer, and review, which enable us to quantify each participant's effectiveness and each translation's quality. These metrics serve as valuable indicators to assess the reliability of participants and facilitate the identification of potential anomalies in translation quality assessment tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate our QAC analysis method using data from machine translation quality assessment experiments, which we conducted to compare different neural translation models.

Intense laser light, when directed at a microsphere, splits into multiple distinct patterns of light, known as eigenchannels. These patterns of light are confined to the surface of the microsphere and are characterized by specific spatial distributions of light intensity. Our study aims to uncover the fundamental properties of these eigenchannels, exploring how they form and what factors influence their behavior. To do this, we use a method that breaks down complex systems into simpler, more manageable components. This approach allows us to understand how different parts of a system, such as individual channels, contribute to the overall behavior of the system. Our findings reveal that each eigenchannel is composed of multiple sub-components, each with its own unique properties. Moreover, we observe that the spatial distribution of light intensity within each eigenchannel is determined by which sub-component is the most dominant. This insight provides a framework for predicting and manipulating the behavior of systems that exhibit complex patterns of light.

Neural networks are prone to contain redundant parameters, which can be removed through parameter-efficient techniques like neural architecture search and weight pruning. A recent study found an interesting connection between these two methods and magnitude pruning's improved generalization performance. We investigate magnitude pruning beyond the neural tangent regime by using an iterative approach. We've found that both neural networks and transformers achieve better results on visual tasks with lower accuracy when trained for a longer time. Notably, we've observed that a significant degree of pruning can lead to restored accuracy on many tasks. We've also discovered that a small number of high-magnitude weights are crucial for low-pruning-fractions and proposed a method called refined magnitude pruning. We've found that this technique results in more compact models with better performance on visual tasks.

This study examines European lotteries, analyzing their structure and the expected profits for operators to determine fair prize allocations. By calculating these profits, the study considers potential inaccuracies and uncertainties in lottery regulations, as well as actual returns based on sold ticket quantities. Given that more informed players often buy fewer tickets than recommended, the study finds that distributing prizes more favorably towards lower-value tickets can be beneficial for players. Furthermore, the study explores correlations between ticket sales and various factors, as well as how sales vary between games.

In the study of the $O(N)$ model with a specific spatial dimension, we expand a specific thermodynamic quantity for large values of an associated parameter, using a well-established theoretical framework. This approach enables us to derive approximate values for critical exponents, and our results are compared with critical exponents from Monte-Carlo simulations. A key observation is that these exponents show a decreasing trend with increasing N. Additionally, we find that the calculated critical exponents align well with those from Monte-Carlo simulations.

In materials science, specifically in the context of two-dimensional hexagonal lattices, our research focuses on how varying strain affects valley Hall transport. We find that a non-uniform strain can break this transport due to the creation of valley-dependent local gauge fields, which can be influenced by mechanical deformations. We calculate the valley Hall conductivity for massless Dirac fermions in a specific type of hexagonal lattice, and discover that it can be quantized under certain conditions. We also examine how the valley Hall conductivity changes with different types of strain and variations in the Fermi energy, and explore how the valley Hall conductivity changes when the underlying symmetry of the lattice is broken.

The domain adaptation (DA) task is designed to enhance the DA model's
generalization ability by combining it with domain-specific information.
However, it has been found that some tasks that use DA as their method for
domain-invariant feature extraction suffer from poor model combination
results, and this is because the way they combine features leads to suboptimal
performance. To address this, this study introduces a new approach that linearly
combines several DA models, referred to as "model soup." The experimental
results show that this method achieves significant improvements, with up to a
10.0% increase in performance on the TextCNN architecture and 10.7% increase
on the Bi-LSTM architecture, both used for text classification.

A key aspect of effective non-linear dimensionality reduction is preserving local proximity in data. This characteristic is particularly significant for spherical data, such as directional measurements, where a Gabor density with an exponential decay is proposed as a more suitable model instead of the Cauchy density used by t-SNE, given that it exhibits heavier tails and an exponential distribution of nearest neighbors. This work presents the derivation and implementation of efficient non-linear dimensionality reduction and manifold learning algorithms tailored for spherical data, employing the Gabor density, along with a variant of the Umeyama algorithm that minimizes distortion in embedded data based on spherical distance. The algorithms are demonstrated using synthetic and real-world data, showcasing improved results. The developed code is publicly available on GitHub.

A new analytical formula has been developed to describe the polaron's self-energy across varying interaction strengths by integrating information about high and low coupling regimes. When applied to a one-particle-hole interaction, the new formula closely matches the exact result for weak interactions but significantly overestimates the result for strong interactions. Furthermore, the new formula reveals that diagrammatic approximations which include multi-particle-hole interactions can be treated independently. As a consequence, the new formula can be used to assess the accuracy of various polaron perturbation theories and estimate the extent of uncertainty in their results.

A digital-analog quantum computing method is proposed to simulate the Fermi-Hubbard model by first using a digital simulator to create its ground state in systems with low dimensions or small sizes, and then employing a Hamiltonian simulator to explore its excited states in systems with higher dimensions or large sizes, potentially achieved with trapped ions.

This research focuses on specific characteristics of matching polynomials for certain graph categories, particularly complete and bipartite graphs, in order to identify these graphs based on this information. A novel approach based on I. Beian's concept of matching polynomial coefficients is proposed to prove relevant conjectures. It turns out that the matching polynomial of a complete graph and a complete bipartite graph can uniquely identify the graph, a property that can be proven using the proposed method. This study also explores the relationship between the matching polynomial of a graph and its complement, leading to the identification of graphs that satisfy specific equations. Furthermore, the study examines the uniqueness of the matching polynomial for trees and binary trees.

The eigenvalues of quantum representations are determined in the star-shaped geometric setting, a concept particularly relevant to understanding pseudo-Anosov elements in the genus-g surface group where g is greater than or equal to 3, for both a specific range of values in the deformed sl(2,C) representation and the standard SL(2,C) representation.

The rapid dissemination of Scrum frameworks along with other agile methods has led to their widespread adoption across numerous industries. As the digital landscape continues to evolve, particularly in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, remote work has become the new norm, prompting organizations to adapt and implement Scrum practices in this new context. Our research aims to delve into the causes and effects of agentic behavior within Scrum frameworks, and to examine how changes in an agent's characteristics can influence their interactions with other agents and the overall system. By applying BDI (Belief-Desire-Intention) modeling, our study explores the dynamics of belief updates and intention revisions under different scenarios, and our findings demonstrate that significant changes in an agent's mental state can lead to the creation of new interactions, even when only a single belief is modified.

This study delves into the eigenvalue problem of the matrix class containing all
square arrowhead matrices of rank one, extending earlier research by Wang et al.
(2019) which initially explored eigenvalues of arrow matrices of rank zero.
Furthermore, this work presents the polynomial eigenfunctions associated with
linear eigenvalue problems involving symmetric arrow matrices of rank one.
These findings may also apply to certain three-term recurrence coefficient matrices
resulting from the discretization of specific second-order differential operators.
In this context, the DG method with $P_1$ finite elements is utilized on unstructured
triangular meshes generated from a single triangle through refinement,
producing rank one modified three-term recurrence matrices that can be
solved analytically.

The proper decay lengths of beauty and charm particles, as well as other sources of background, have been determined using the ATLAS detector at the LHC. Beauty and charm particles were identified through the use of the ATLAS track-finder, which analyzed distributions of displaced vertices, and the use of flight directions in data collected from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 and 13 TeV. The analysis, which utilized data from both energy levels, yielded the mean proper decay lengths: $495 \pm 7 \pm 5$ $\mu$m for beauty particles, $233 \pm 10 \pm 4 \pm 10$ $\mu$m for charm particles, and $299 \pm 10 \pm 4 \pm 5$ $\mu$m for background particles. The results, which are consistent with the Standard Model of particle physics, have been published in the Journal of High Energy Physics.
